entries.topic: How the federal district was made

claims.text: The Residence Act was signed 16 July 1790 after a dinner bargain at Jefferson's house among Hamilton, Jefferson and Madison: the national government would assume the states' debts and the capital would sit on the Potomac; Philadelphia served as capital for the ten-year interim, and by autumn 1800 only the President's House, the Capitol's north wing and the avenue between them were usable. Alexandria was returned to Virginia in 1846.

The Organic Act of 1871 reorganized the government of Washington, DC, ending the separate charters of Washington and Georgetown; its language constituting a municipal corporation is common for cities; the claim that it made the United States a corporation is false (rated Pants on Fire, 12 February 2024) and was popularized by the "sovereign citizens" movement.

The DC flag is based on the Washington family coat of arms (three red stars over two red bars on white, per Mount Vernon); a 2023 claim that its stars stand for a "three-city empire" of DC, London and the Vatican was rated Pants on Fire (3 May 2023).

entries.topic: How DC is governed: Home Rule and its limits

claims.text: Home Rule Act signed 24 December 1973 by President Nixon (Pub. L. 93-198): elected mayor and a 13-member council. The council may not impose a commuter tax, change the Height of Buildings Act of 1910, change the composition or jurisdiction of the local courts, lend public credit for private projects or pass an unbalanced budget, and gains no authority over the National Capital Planning Commission, the Washington Aqueduct or the DC National Guard. Congress reviews all council legislation and retains authority over the budget. Disapproval used four times: 1979, 1981, 1990, 2023. In February 2025 the BOWSER Act was introduced to repeal Home Rule.

DC's locally raised budget must go through congressional appropriations, which has been used to bar local spending on a needle exchange and marijuana commercialization; review periods are 30 days and 60 days for crime laws; the federal government retains control of DC's courts and prosecutor; Congress blocked the city's criminal-code revision.

DC courts were created by Congress in 1970 under Article I; the President appoints judges with Senate consent from three names per vacancy sent by the DC Judicial Nomination Commission, for 15-year terms; the Superior Court has a chief judge and 61 associate judges; as of 1 November 2023 it had 12 vacancies. The US Attorney's Office for DC prosecutes most crimes; the DC Attorney General a limited set (juvenile, municipal); prisoners sentenced to more than a year go to the Federal Bureau of Prisons; appropriations come through Congress's Financial Services and General Government subcommittees.

Executive Order 14333, 11 August 2025, declared a crime emergency and invoked Section 740 of the Home Rule Act for the first time to direct the Metropolitan Police; that direction expired 10 September 2025; DC sued on 15 August 2025. National Guard deployed from August 2025 with Guard units from several Republican-governed states. On 20 November 2025 Judge Jia Cobb held the deployment unlawful; the DC Circuit stayed her order (administrative stay 4 December, panel stay 17 December 2025).

On 14 October 2026 a DC Circuit panel (Pillard, Rogers, Garcia) heard argument; about 2,900 Guard troops were in DC, down from nearly 5,000 in the summer; the Defense Department extended the mission to January 2029; the stay keeps the Guard in place pending decision.

claims.text: The United States imposed an arms embargo in November 1947 covering the Jews of Palestine and the Arab states; critics argued it fell most heavily on the Jews, who had no state yet.

Marshall's memorandum of the White House meeting of 12 May 1948 (with Truman, Lovett, Clifford, Niles, Connelly): Clifford's suggestions were "wrong", "based on domestic political considerations", a "transparent dodge to win a few votes"; "if the President were to follow Mr. Clifford's advice and if in the elections I were to vote, I would vote against the President."

claims.text: Through FY2025 the US provided about $175 billion in current dollars (Table 1: $174.97 billion: $124.5 billion military, $34.3 billion economic, $16.1 billion missile defense); about $298 billion in constant 2024 dollars for 1946–2024. MOUs: 1999 (FY1999–2008, at least $26.7 billion including $21.3 billion military); 2007 (FY2009–2018, $30 billion, up to 26.3% spendable in Israel); 2016 (signed 14 September 2016, FY2019–2028, $38 billion: $33 billion FMF and $5 billion missile defense). P.L. 118-50 (April 2024): $3.5 billion FMF, $4 billion missile defense, $1.2 billion Iron Beam. 2008 Naval Vessel Transfer Act defined the qualitative military edge. WRSA-I stockpile in Israel; P.L. 119-4 authorizes $500 million a year additions through FY2027.

Kennedy approved the Hawk sale over State Department objections; Johnson's Phantom sale made the US Israel's principal arms supplier; 1981 strategic cooperation memorandum, suspended 18 December 1981 over the Golan annexation; 1987 major non-NATO ally designation.

Next MOU: formal talks opened the week of 1 June 2026 with the stated goal of moving "from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership"; US team led by Ambassador Huckabee and Counselor Holler, Israeli team by Defense Ministry Director-General Amir Baram and Ambassador Yechiel Leiter.

On 3 November 2026 Trump said US military aid to Israel would end by the end of the year; on 9 November Rubio said Trump "would like for the financing portion to end as soon as possible" and that "we'll negotiate the timeline"; the current MOU provides $3.8 billion a year to the end of September 2028. Ynet reported on 9 November a draft extending FMF at $3.3 billion a year for five years after 2028, then phasing it out; not finalized.

entries.topic: The veto at the Security Council

claims.text: The Jewish Virtual Library lists 51 US vetoes of draft resolutions critical of Israel, from 10 September 1972 (S/10784, Lebanon) to 18 September 2025 (S/2025/583); examples include 18 February 2011 (settlements), 18 December 2017 (Jerusalem), 8 December 2023 (Gaza ceasefire) and 18 April 2024 (Palestinian UN membership).

On 18 September 2025 the US cast the only vote against a draft demanding an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire, release of all hostages and lifting of aid restrictions; the US had vetoed five earlier ceasefire drafts since the war began.

sources.label: Jewish Virtual Library, "U.S. Vetoes of UN Security Council Resolutions Critical to Israel"

claims.text: The Biden administration held a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs around May 2024 over concern about their use in densely populated Rafah, described as the first US restriction of military support in the war; on 25 January 2025 the Trump White House released them ("ordered and paid for by Israel... now on their way").
